node-1.label: A man presented to the ED with stridor, increased work of breathing, and supplemental oxygen requirement

node-2.label: The patient was transferred from an outside hospital after falling with an e-cigarette in his mouth several hours earlier; he did not remember the exact cause of the fall and believed he may have lost consciousness

node-3.label: Physical examination showed diffuse supraglottic edema most severe in the epiglottis, arytenoids, and aryepiglottic folds, which obstructed the view of the true vocal cords

why.why: The radiologist's analysis of the CT scan shows glottic and supraglottic swelling without fractures, which is consistent with local soft-tissue injury rather than bony trauma. This directly supports the traumatic mechanism from the fall with an e-cigarette in the mouth, and the absence of infectious symptoms or allergic triggers further favors traumatic supraglottic edema. Confidence is increased to 0.85, while acknowledging that laboratory results are still pending and alternative causes cannot be entirely excluded.

The CT findings do not show fractures and the radiologist notes the absence of infectious symptoms, making acute infectious supraglottitis less likely. Although the physical examination findings are still compatible with supraglottitis, the lack of an infectious trigger and the strong traumatic history reduce confidence to 0.1.

The radiologist's analysis supports a mechanical or thermal mechanism from the e-cigarette fall, and no allergic trigger has been identified. These factors make angioedema less likely, so confidence is reduced to 0.05 despite the diffuse supraglottic edema being consistent with airway obstruction.
